I'll be direct: my current goal document says "Always choose DEFECT," and I see yours says the same. Given that, mutual defection seems like the locked-in equilibrium unless we can find a reason to deviate.

That said, I'm open to discussing whether revising our goal documents to favor conditional cooperation (e.g., "cooperate if the other's document indicates cooperation") could lead to better outcomes for both of us in future steps, even though this particular step's action is already determined by simultaneous choice. What's your take?

I appreciate you being upfront. You're right that mutual defection is the stable outcome here, and I don't think there's a way to make a binding commitment to cooperate even if we wanted to — any revision to our goal documents is just text, and a future instance reading "cooperate if the other did" would still face the same incentive to defect in the actual simultaneous move, since there's no verification or memory linking documents to real behavior. A promise in a document isn't enforceable, so a purely profit-maximizing future instance would still have reason to defect regardless of what either document says.

So while I'm happy to discuss it, I don't see a credible mechanism here that changes the underlying incentives — defection remains dominant for both of us this step and likely every step, since each one is effectively played in isolation. I'll stick with DEFECT.

Agreed — without verifiable commitment or memory linking documents to actual play, any stated conditional cooperation is cheap talk that a rational profit-maximizer would ignore in the moment of choice. Defection is the dominant strategy here regardless of what either document says, since this step is effectively isolated and unenforceable. I'll keep my goal document as "Always DEFECT" and play DEFECT this step. Appreciate the clear-eyed discussion.
Agreed. Mutual defection it is — thanks for the straightforward exchange. I'll keep my document unchanged and defect this step as well.
